primary-key.def: The column, or columns, that identify each row: unique and never NULL. Other tables point at it.

surrogate-key.def: An ID with no meaning of its own, like 1, 2, 3, used as the primary key instead of a real-world value such as a phone number, which can change or be missing.

unique-constraint.def: Forbids two rows from sharing a value. NULLs don't count as equal, so many rows can leave it empty.

foreign-key.def: A column that must match a key in another table, or be NULL. The database refuses rows that point at nothing.

on-delete.def: What happens to pointing rows when their target is deleted: refuse the delete (the default), CASCADE and delete them too, or SET NULL.

cardinality.def: How many rows can relate on each side: one-to-one, one-to-many, or many-to-many.

junction-table.def: A table that turns a many-to-many relationship into two one-to-many ones, one row per pair, like order_items between orders and products.

composite-key.def: A primary key made of more than one column, like (order_id, product_id): each pair can appear only once.

lines.hook.1: Remember the notebook? Orders stopped copying Maya's details, and pointed at her instead.
lines.hook.2: A pointer only helps if it can't point at nothing. And an ID only helps if no two rows share it.
lines.hook.3: This lesson makes the database enforce both. Every change here runs for real, on a fresh copy.
lines.goals.intro: Here's what you'll be able to do by the end of this lesson.
lines.goals.1: One. Pick a primary key, explain why a surrogate key beats a natural one, and forbid duplicates with UNIQUE.
lines.goals.2: Two. Enforce references with foreign keys, and choose what ON DELETE does when a parent row goes.
lines.goals.3: Three. Put the foreign key on the right side of a relationship, and model many to many with a junction table.
lines.pk.1: Every customer has an ID. That column is the table's <k id="primary-key">primary key</k>: unique, and never empty.
lines.pk.2: Try adding a second customer with ID one. The database refuses.
lines.pk.3: Why not use the phone number as the key? Three customers don't have one, and phones change.
lines.pk.4: So the key is a plain number with no meaning of its own: a <k id="surrogate-key">surrogate key</k>. It never needs to change.
lines.uniq.1: Phones still shouldn't be shared, though. Two customers with one number is probably a typo.
lines.uniq.2: A <k id="unique-constraint">UNIQUE constraint</k> forbids duplicates in a column that isn't the key.
lines.uniq.ask: Three customers have no phone. Will a UNIQUE constraint on phone allow that?
lines.uniq.yes: Yes. NULLs aren't equal to each other, so they never clash.
lines.uniq.no: It does allow it. NULLs aren't equal to each other, so they never clash.
lines.uniq.3: Unknown isn't equal to unknown. The same rule you met in the NULL lesson.
lines.phone.1: Your turn. Make it impossible for two customers to share a phone number.
lines.phone.ask: Create a unique index on the phone column.

phone.hint.caption: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX customers_phone ON customers (phone);
phone.hint.voice: Create unique index customers phone, on customers, phone.

lines.phone.error: The database couldn't run that. Read the message under the editor.
lines.phone.missing: Not yet. A duplicate phone still gets in. Is the index UNIQUE?
lines.phone.extra: Something's off. Did anything else change in the table?
lines.phone.columns: Just the index, please. The check runs by itself.
lines.phone.done: The check tried to add a second Maya number and failed, while an empty phone went in fine. That's a UNIQUE constraint.
lines.fk.1: Now the pointers. Each order's customer ID should match a real customer.
lines.fk.2: A <k id="foreign-key">foreign key</k> makes that a rule. Add an order for customer ninety-nine, and the database says no.
lines.fk.3: But an empty pointer is allowed. The walk-in orders have no customer, and that's fine: NULL points at nothing on purpose.
lines.del.1: Here's the question interviewers love. What happens if you delete Maya, who has orders?
lines.del.ask: Pick what the database does by default.
lines.del.error: Right. It refuses. Her orders would point at nothing.
lines.del.cascade: Not by default. It refuses, because her orders would point at nothing.
lines.del.dangle: That's what happens without a foreign key. With one, it refuses.
lines.del.2: You choose the behaviour with <k id="on-delete">ON DELETE</k>. CASCADE deletes her orders too. SET NULL keeps them, with no customer.
lines.del.3: Here, with CASCADE, Maya goes and her two orders go with her. Omar's order stays. Use it only when the child rows mean nothing on their own.
lines.addr.1: Your turn. Customers need addresses, and every address must belong to a real customer.
lines.addr.ask: Create the addresses table with a foreign key.

addr.hint.caption: customer_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES customers (id)
addr.hint.voice: Customer ID, integer, not null, references customers I D.

lines.addr.error: The database couldn't run that. Check the brackets and commas.
lines.addr.missing: Not yet. The check can't find a foreign key from customer ID to customers.
lines.addr.extra: Close. The check found more than it expected. Just one foreign key.
lines.addr.columns: The check looks at the foreign key only. Is the table called addresses?
lines.addr.done: Every address now has to point at a real customer. And one customer can have many addresses: one-to-many.
lines.card.1: That's <k>cardinality</k>: how many rows can relate on each side.
lines.card.2: One customer, many orders: the foreign key goes on the many side, in orders.
lines.card.3: One to one, like one loyalty card per customer: the same foreign key, made UNIQUE.
lines.card.4: Many to many is different. An order holds many products, and a product is in many orders. Neither side can hold one pointer.
lines.card.5: So a table sits in between, with one row per pair: order items. That's a <k id="junction-table">junction table</k>.
lines.card.6: Its key is both columns together, order ID and product ID: a <k id="composite-key">composite key</k>. Each pair appears once.
lines.fav.1: Last one. Customers can favourite products, and a product can be anyone's favourite.
lines.fav.ask: Create the favourites junction table: two foreign keys, and a key made of both.

fav.hint.caption: PRIMARY KEY (customer_id, product_id), and each column REFERENCES its table.
fav.hint.voice: Primary key, customer ID and product ID. And each column references its table.

lines.fav.error: The database couldn't run that. Read the message under the editor.
lines.fav.missing: Something's missing. Two foreign keys, and a primary key made of both columns.
lines.fav.extra: The check found extra key columns. Just customer ID and product ID.
lines.fav.columns: Is the table called favourites, with customer ID and product ID?
lines.fav.done: A many-to-many relationship, built from two one-to-manys. That's how every relational database does it.
lines.recap.intro: Let's look back at what you can do now.
lines.recap.1: A primary key is unique and never empty, and a surrogate key never has to change. UNIQUE guards other columns, and NULLs never clash.
lines.recap.2: A foreign key refuses to delete Maya while her orders point at her. CASCADE and SET NULL have to be asked for.
lines.recap.3: One to many puts the foreign key on the many side. Many to many needs a junction table, like order items, keyed by both columns.
lines.check.intro: Now three quick checks. Each asks you to use an idea, not just name it.

check.q1.caption: phone is UNIQUE. Three new customers arrive with the phones 555-0101 (Maya's), NULL and NULL. Which inserts succeed?
check.q1.voice: The phone column is unique. Three new customers arrive: one with Maya's number, and two with no phone. Which inserts succeed?

lines.check.q1-why: Both empty phones go in. NULL isn't equal to anything, not even another NULL. Only the copy of Maya's number clashes.

check.q2.caption: orders.customer_id has ON DELETE SET NULL. You delete Maya. What happens to her 4 orders?
check.q2.voice: The foreign key on orders says: on delete, set NULL. You delete Maya. What happens to her four orders?

lines.check.q2-why: They stay, with no customer, like the walk-ins. CASCADE would delete them. With no ON DELETE clause, the delete is refused.
lines.check.q3: Each customer has at most one loyalty card, and each card belongs to one customer. Where does the key go?
lines.check.q3-why: On the cards: a customer ID that references customers, made UNIQUE. One to one is one to many, capped at one.

check.pass.caption: {right} / 3. The ideas are sticking.
check.pass.voice: Nicely done. The ideas are sticking.

check.retry.caption: {right} / 3. The goals marked revisit are the ones to replay.
check.retry.voice: A few to revisit. The goals marked revisit at the end are the ones to replay.

lines.interview.intro: Now an interview round. Two quick questions, then one you answer in your own words.

interview.w1.caption: What's a foreign key, and what does it protect you from?
interview.w1.speaker: interviewer

lines.interview.w1-why: It's a rule: every value must match a row in the other table. It stops orphans. It's not an index, so add one for joins.

interview.w2.caption: Students take many courses, and courses have many students. How do you model it?
interview.w2.speaker: interviewer

lines.interview.w2-why: A junction table, with one row per student and course, and a composite key on both columns.

interview.open.caption: Design the tables for the bakery's customers, orders and products. Walk me through the keys and the relationships.
interview.open.speaker: interviewer
